newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa ex-foreign minister Pik Botha lied -police.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa ex-foreign minister Pik Botha lied -police.

text.p: An apartheid-era secret policeman on Tuesday accused former foreign minister Pik Botha of having lied to the world about a car bomb that South African agents planted in the Botswana capital Gaborone 10 years ago.

Brigadier Jack Cronje, now retired, made the accusation in an application for amnesty to the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, which is trying to uncover human rights abuses during the apartheid years.

The car bomb, which exploded in April 1987, killed a woman and two children. Botswana protested to neighbouring South Africa at the time but Botha responded that the explosion was the fault of the African National Congress (ANC), which was then fighting a guerrilla war against his government.
Cronje told the truth commission he had been involved in rigging the minibus bomb, which was intended to kill a leading ANC guerrilla based in Botswana, Johannes Mnisi.
The bomb was fitted in a secret compartment and was set to detonate if the compartment was opened. It could also be set off by remote control, Cronje said.

He said a security police informer, Keith MacKenzie, drove the minibus to Gaborone for delivery to Mnisi. But the ANC knew they could not trust MacKenzie and sent him to a detention camp in Angola where he was tortured, Cronje said.

"The whole plan then went wrong," he said. "I learned from newspapers that the bomb went off in an unplanned way... the Botswana government lodged a formal complaint with the South African government.

"Botha alleged that MacKenzie was a member of the ANC and that they themselves blew up their own vehicle. I have no doubt that Minister Botha must in fact have known what the true situation was," Cronje said.
No immediate comment was available on Tuesday from Botha, who served as energy and mineral affairs minister in President Nelson Mandela's government of national unity until his retirement last year.
Cronje's evidence was the first to name Botha as having direct knowledge of the covert actions of the security forces against black liberation groups.
Cronje said General Johann van der Merwe, who served as police commissioner in the early 1990s, also had full knowledge of the plan to kill Mnisi.
Cronje, explaining the motives of the security police in the late 1980s when the ANC's guerrilla war was reaching a peak, said high-profile black opposition leaders had to be "eliminated".
